Java question regarding learning (to do with the Google vs Oracle situation)

Personally, I don't think you should be worried, given Java is huge behemoth and will not easily vanish in my opinion. If you are still worried, however, you should feel comfortable continuing with C#. In fact, C# and Java are very similar, and I'd say if you know C#, you will already implicitly know Java. Remember that Java is very corporate, and can't move as fast as C# could. As a result, I see C# as an improvement over Java, in a sense that it can do the exact same plus more. If you're comfortable with C#, you will have no trouble learning Java's syntax in less than a day, in case you really want to make that Android application.

The other way around, from Java to C#, might take you a wee bit more time, given there are more things to learn like properties, generators (yield), operator overloading and such. As a final remark, I'd like to say that .NET is turning more cross-platform friendly by the day with Roslyn, and you may use ASP.NET for creating web applications. These days there's a huge circlejerk concerning scalability. In practice, however, it often doesn't matter, as in many cases the bottlenecks lie somewhere else, if that amount of data throughput is even met. By the time it actually becomes a problem, you should look into how things can get improved or not. Of course, it doesn't hurt to create your service / program with optimization and scalability in your mind, but it shouldn't be a primary concern unless you're Amazon. Pre-mature optimization is the root of all evil; first get it to work, optimize (or scale) later.

How to light a Fire ANY CONDITION, ANYTIME, ANYWHERE

Found this in the comments since I hate watching slow-paced videos, no matter how interesting or useful the information.

A low cross-sectional density combined with the most available surface area yields the best heat transfer through the material, allowing it to come up to the critical combustion heat range, faster. A thin edge will always light faster than a thicker rounded edge because of this principle.

The second principle is a ready and easily available source of oxygen. A fire has to breathe, and the easier it breathes, the faster and hotter it burns. Fire is a form of rapid oxidation of the fuel material. A loose pile a material has more readily available oxygen than a tightly packed pile of fuel, and therefore will always burn better.

The Third principle is that heat rises and cold sinks. Fire climbs objects faster than it descends them because heat rises. The heat from the flame below heats the objects above it to combustion temperature rapidly, and tends to start a system into effect called convection. The hot gasses rise, sucking in cold air from below, further oxygenating the fire.

The teepee fire lay, log cabin style pyramid lay, and any other fire lay which allows the heat below to rapidly heat the fuel above while still leaving enough gaps in the material to rapidly and easily oxidize is a good lay for adverse conditions. I prefer the teepee lay as well for the worst conditions, but for a reason. The shape of the teepee lay provides for rapid drainage on the outside of the fuel directly to the ground for any stray moisture which may collect as you attempt to get the fire to a sustainable point.

-Paul Andrulis
